source.title: Spectral bias and task-model alignment explain generalization in kernel regression and infinitely wide neural networks
source.authors: Abdulkadir Canatar; Blake Bordelon; Cengiz Pehlevan

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and supplementary information are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study analytically derives and experimentally examines sample-size learning curves for kernel regression and infinitely wide neural networks. This is a conceptual test of sample-wise non-monotonic generalization, using a different method and model class from the original deep-network size and epoch sweeps.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's own sample-size generalization results, including explicit noise and regularization conditions. Results cited from other studies and quantities used only to characterize spectra or select experimental settings are not included.
record.test_reason: The study derives and simulates sample-size learning curves for kernel regression, a different method from the deep-network originals. Its own results bear directly on V3 (more data can hurt near the interpolation threshold). They also bear on V6: peaks need label noise or out-of-RKHS effective noise, are variance-driven, can recur once per learning stage, and vanish at the optimal ridge λ* = σ².
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also derive an optimal ridge λ* = σ², independent of sample size, that removes the peak. They state the white band-limited peak is due to overfitting noisy labels rather than initialization variance, and that it disappears without noise.
record.recipe_differences: Uses replica-method theory and kernel-regression experiments, including infinite-width NTK comparisons; it does not reproduce the original deep-network model-size or epoch interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Peak occurrence and magnitude depend on label or effective noise, explicit or implicit regularization, kernel spectrum, target alignment or out-of-RKHS components, and learning stage.
record.problems: The main evidence is for kernel-regression settings, not broad finite-width deep-network capacity sweeps. Some conclusions are analytical or communicated through plots without numerical peak values in the text. The authors note that the kernel theory has limited applicability to state-of-the-art networks outside the kernel regime, and that finite-width network learning curves depart from NTK predictions at some sample sizes.

untested.parts: Tested only in kernel regression and the infinite-width NTK limit. There are no finite-width deep-network sample sweeps showing a peak, and the finite-network comparison in Fig. 6a is not reported as a peak result.
No sweep of capacity past the interpolation point. Peaks are along sample count, located at P = N or P ~ N(D,L).
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across size, epochs and samples. The peak location α ≈ 1 + λ̃_L is derived only along the sample axis.
No re-counting of parameters to turn a second descent into a U-shape.

missing.what: Bias–variance decomposition showing the non-monotonicity comes solely from the variance term, with the divergence at α = 1 due to variance
Regularization sweep at fixed effective noise: larger λ̃ suppresses peaks, and the optimal setting gives no double descent in the first learning stage
Analytic phase boundary σ² > g(λ) for non-monotonicity, with the peak at α ≈ 1 + λ that approaches α = 1 + λ at high noise
Power-law kernel (η̄_k = k^-8, D = 20): double descent at stage k appears only when σ̃² > g(λ̃_k)
NTK regression and 2-layer ReLU network (50000 units) learning curves at noise levels chosen by g(λ). The network departs from NTK at large P.
Faster-decaying spectra are more prone to peaks, and higher learning stages are more immune because effective regularization λ̃_L grows with L
missing.locator: Multiple Learning Episodes section; Fig. 5a; Supplementary Note 4

record.verdict_notes: This is a theory-plus-simulation study whose evidence is largely the authors' own figures, with few numeric peak values given in the text. Neither original source is among the study's authors. The V6 mechanism here is noise variance in a kernel setting with no random-feature initialization variance; the authors contrast this with random-features peaks.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep testing whether test error falls, peaks near the training-set fitting threshold, and falls again.
No test-error curve over training epochs or other training-time steps.
Tests sample-size increases in kernel-regression settings; it does not test the claim across arbitrary model classes or establish that the effect occurs in all settings.
Does not sweep model capacity across model classes to test risk as capacity grows past an interpolation point.
Does not test a single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.

Tests label noise, out-of-RKHS target components, regularization, and multiple sample-wise peaks in specified kernel settings; it does not establish these effects for every model class or training axis.
Does not test whether re-counting complexity by an effective parameter count turns a second-descent curve into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: White band-limited RKHS kernel regression
rows.size_stated: N = 800 in the simulation; theoretical model has N equal nonzero eigenvalues
rows.operation_detail: Measured generalization error over α at the analytically optimal ridge value.
rows.baseline: Other ridge values at the same noise level; no numerical baseline value stated.
rows.value: λ* = σ² minimizes generalization error for every α and gives a monotonic learning curve.
rows.uncertainty: Error bars describe standard deviation over 15 trials in the illustrated simulations.
rows.locator: Main text, Double-Descent Phase Transition in a Band-Limited RKHS; Fig. 3c–d; Supplementary Note 3
rows.note: The optimality and monotonicity are stated analytically; the figure illustrates the result.
rows.check: The baseline should be the noisy curves at sub-optimal or zero ridge, which have a peak (Fig. 3c). The analytic claim is that λ* = σ² is optimal at every α and gives a monotone curve, which matches V6's claim that optimal regularization removes the peak.

relationships.condition: No effective noise, or ridge at or above the optimum λ* = σ² (more generally, noise below the phase boundary g(λ))
relationships.reason: Learning curves are monotone in these conditions, so more data hurts only when effective noise exceeds g(λ) (R3, R5, R6).

source_check.condition: No effective noise, or ridge at or above the optimum λ* = σ² (more generally, noise below the phase boundary g(λ))
source_check.reason: R3 and R5 establish monotone noiseless curves; R6 establishes monotonicity at optimal ridge. The Eq. (8) boundary is piecewise: g(λ) for λ < 1 and 2λ + 1 for λ ≥ 1.

relationships.condition: White band-limited, Gaussian RBF (real and synthetic data) and rotation-invariant kernel regression
relationships.reason: Peaks appear only with label or out-of-RKHS noise and come from estimator variance. Multiple stage-wise peaks are possible, and the optimal ridge λ* = σ² gives monotone curves (R1–R9).
relationships.display_finding: Peaks required label noise or signal outside the RKHS and arose from estimator variance; multiple stage-wise peaks were possible, while optimal λ* = σ² yielded monotone curves.
